title: Learn by Doing: Pipelining and Hazards
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on pipelining and hazards, each worked and then taught from nothing.
intro: Part A is the objective questions on this topic, the largest group in the whole bank. Part B is past questions only, and the four phase pipeline with latch delay has been set in consecutive years with the same durations, 60, 50, 90 and 80 ns.

lockin.big: "The clock is the slowest stage plus the latch delay. k stages, n instructions, time is k plus n minus 1 cycles."
lockin.sub: Speedup approaches the number of stages and never exceeds it. Structural, data and control hazards, and forwarding fixes most data hazards.

methodFrames.teach: Pipelining overlaps instructions: while one is being executed, the next is being decoded and a third fetched. Nothing runs faster; more is in flight at once, so throughput rises.
methodFrames.ask: Four stages take 60, 50, 90 and 80 ns. How long can the clock cycle be?

methodFrames.check: At least 90 ns, the slowest stage.
methodFrames.teach: Every stage shares one clock, so the slowest stage sets the cycle. Add the latch delay between stages: with a 10 ns latch the cycle is 100 ns. That addition is where most marks are dropped.
methodFrames.ask: Without the pipeline, how long does one instruction take through those four stages?

methodFrames.check: 60 plus 50 plus 90 plus 80, which is 280 ns.
methodFrames.teach: So a non pipelined machine takes n times 280 ns for n instructions. The pipelined one fills up first: the first instruction leaves after k cycles, and each one after it leaves one cycle later.
methodFrames.ask: Write the general formula for n instructions in a k stage pipeline.

methodFrames.teach: Then multiply by the cycle time. Speedup is the non pipelined time divided by the pipelined time, and as n grows it approaches k, the number of stages, which it never exceeds.
methodFrames.ask: For 1000 instructions here: pipelined time, and speedup?

methodFrames.check: (4 plus 999) times 100 ns, which is 100.3 microseconds, against 280 microseconds, so a speedup of about 2.79.
methodFrames.teach: Note it is well short of 4, because of the latch and the uneven stages. Say that in a sentence: an unbalanced pipeline wastes the difference between the slowest stage and the others, every cycle.
methodFrames.ask: Now hazards. An instruction needs a result the one before it has not yet written. What is that called, and what type?

methodFrames.check: A data hazard, of the read after write kind.
methodFrames.teach: Three families: structural, two instructions wanting the same hardware; data, an operand not ready, in RAW, WAR and WAW forms; control, a branch whose outcome is not yet known. RAW is the one that happens in a simple pipeline.
methodFrames.ask: Two fixes for a data hazard, one cheap and one that costs cycles.

methodFrames.check: Forwarding the result straight from one stage to the next, or stalling until it is written.
methodFrames.teach: Forwarding, also called bypassing, sends the ALU result back into the next instruction's input without waiting for the write back, and it removes most RAW stalls. A load followed immediately by a use still costs one stall. For control hazards: branch prediction, delayed branches, or flushing what was fetched wrongly.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Q1(b)

scenario.text: b. A computer manufacturer is evaluating whether to replace a non-pipelined processor with a five-stage pipelined processor. The processor executes the following instruction mix: Arithmetic – 40%, Memory Access – 35%, Branch – 20%, Floating Point – 5%. The Non-pipelined processor clock cycle is 25ns. Pipelined processor stage times are: IF – 5ns, ID – 4ns, EX – 6ns, MEM – 5ns and WB – 4ns. Furthermore, Pipeline register overhead is 1 ns. Branch instructions incur a two-cycle penalty, Floating-point instructions has three cycles for EX stage, Memory accesses experience cache misses 10% of the time, adding four extra cycles. The program contains 20 million instructions. i) Determine the pipelined clock cycle. 1mk ii) Calculate the actual CPI. 2mks iii) Determine the actual execution time. 1mk iv) Compute the speedup over the non-pipelined processor. 1mk v) Explain why the speedup differs from the theoretical maximum. 1mk

questions.asked: Set once, in 2025/2026. It is still the examiner's own question, and the method behind it is on the syllabus.

exam.problem: Given mix arithmetic 40%, memory 35%, branch 20%, floating point 5% ; five stage times 5, 4, 6, 5, 4 ns ; register overhead 1 ns ; non-pipelined clock 25 ns ; IC = 20 000 000 ; branch adds a 2-cycle penalty, floating point adds 4 extra cycles, a memory access misses 10% of the time adding 4 more.
exam.answer:
Find pipelined clock, actual CPI, execution time, speedup, and why it is short of the max
Formula clock = slowest stage + overhead · actual CPI = 1 + Σ(fraction × extra cycles) · time = IC × CPI × T · speedup = time(non-pipe) / time(pipe)

The stem is dense and does not say whether each penalty is extra or total, so state the reading: base CPI 1; branch +2; memory +(2 + 0.10×4) = 2.4; floating point +4; arithmetic +0.

Clock  = max(5,4,6,5,4) + overhead
       = 6 + 1 = 7 ns

CPI    = 1                (base, one per cycle)
       + 0.20 x 2         (branch)
       + 0.35 x 2.4       (memory: 2 + 0.10x4)
       + 0.05 x 4         (floating point)
       + 0.40 x 0         (arithmetic)
       = 1 + 0.40 + 0.84 + 0.20
       = 2.44

Time   = IC x CPI x T
       = 20,000,000 x 2.44 x 7 ns = 0.3416 s
Non-pipe = 20,000,000 x 25 ns    = 0.5 s
Speedup  = 0.5 / 0.3416          = 1.46
Clock 7 ns; CPI 2.44; time 0.3416 s; speedup 1.46. (v) It is far below the ideal 5 because the branch, floating-point and cache-miss penalties and the register overhead all raise the CPI above 1.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Q2(b)

scenario.text: b. Consider the following code segment executed on a classic five-stage RISC processor. I1: LW R1,0(R2) I2: ADD R3,R1,R4 I3: SUB R5,R3,R6 I4: SW R5,8(R2) I5: BEQ R5,R0,LABEL I6: MUL R7,R5,R8 Assume: • forwarding is available • branch resolved in EX stage • load-use hazards require one stall • multiplier occupies EX for three cycles • separate instruction and data caches i) Identify and explain every pipeline hazard. 5mks ii) Draw the pipeline timing diagram 2mks iii) Determine the total execution cycles 1mk iv) Suggest any two hardware improvements that would reduce stalls. 1mk

exam.problem: Given six instructions on a classic 5-stage RISC pipeline ; forwarding on ; branch resolved in EX ; load-use costs 1 stall ; MUL holds EX for 3 cycles ; separate caches
exam.answer:
Find the hazards, the timing diagram, the total cycles, two improvements
Formula ideal = (k + n − 1) cycles, then add every stall: 1 per load-use, and (EX cycles − 1) per multi-cycle execute

Hazards

I1→I2 is a load-use RAW (R1 not ready until MEM, so I2 stalls one cycle). I2→I3, I3→I4, I3→I5, I3→I6 are ordinary RAW hazards hidden by forwarding. I6's multiply holds EX for three cycles, adding two extra at the end. Structural hazards are avoided by the separate caches.

Timing diagram (one stall, then the long multiply)

Cyc12345678910111213
I1 LWIFIDEXMEWB
I2 ADDIFID--EXMEWB
I3 SUBIF--IDEXMEWB
I4 SWIFIDEXMEWB
I5 BEQIFIDEXMEWB
I6 MULIFIDEXEXEXMEWB
One load-use stall (the -- in cycle 4) plus two extra multiply cycles give a total of 13 cycles (a clean run of 6 would be 5 + 6 − 1 = 10). Two improvements: add more forwarding paths, and pipeline or duplicate the multiplier.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Q3(b)

scenario.text: b. A 5-stage pipelined processor has instruction fetch (IF), Instruction decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Execute (Ex) and Write Back (WB) stages. The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for any instruction. The PO stage take 1 cycle for ADD and SUB instructions, 3 clock cycles for MUL instruction and 6 clock cycles for DIV instruction respectively. Operand forwarding is used in the pipeline. Draw the cycle diagram and determine the number of cycles needed to execute the following sequence of instructions: i. When Operand forwarding is used 4½mks ii. When Operand forwarding is not used 5½mks I1 MUL R2, R0, R1 ; R2 ← R0 X R1 I2 DIV R5, R3, R4 ; R5 ← R3/R4 I3 ADD R2, R5, R2 ; R2 ← R5 + R2 I4 SUB R5, R2, R6 ; R5 ← R2 – R6

exam.problem: Given 5 stages IF, ID, OF, EX, WB, one cycle each except EX = 1 (ADD/SUB), 3 (MUL), 6 (DIV) ; four instructions ; do it with and without forwarding
exam.answer:
Find the cycle diagram and total cycles for each case
Formula no single formula once EX is multi-cycle: lay the schedule out cycle by cycle, a long EX blocks those behind it, then read the total off the last write-back

The paper prints "PO stage", struck through in pen to EX. Instructions: I1 MUL R2,R0,R1 ; I2 DIV R5,R3,R4 ; I3 ADD R2,R5,R2 (needs R5 from I2 and R2 from I1) ; I4 SUB R5,R2,R6 (needs R2 from I3). Read each cell as the stage that instruction is in that cycle; "--" is a stall.

(i) With operand forwarding

Instr123456789101112131415
I1 MULIFIDOFEXEXEXWB
I2 DIVIFIDOF----EXEXEXEXEXEXWB
I3 ADDIFID----OF----------EXWB
I4 SUBIF----ID----------OFEXWB

The DIV holds EX for six cycles (7 to 12) and blocks everything behind it. With forwarding, I3 takes R5 straight from I2's EX and runs at cycle 13, and I4 takes R2 from I3 and runs at 14, so the last write-back is at cycle 15.

(ii) Without operand forwarding

Instr1234567891011121314151617
I1 MULIFIDOFEXEXEXWB
I2 DIVIFIDOF----EXEXEXEXEXEXWB
I3 ADDIFID----OF------------EXWB
I4 SUBIF----ID--------------OFEXWB

Without forwarding, I3 must wait for I2's write-back before it can read R5 (one cycle later, EX at 14), and I4 likewise waits for I3, so the last write-back slips to cycle 17.

Total = 15 cycles with forwarding, 17 cycles without. Forwarding saved 2 cycles here.

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Given 4 phases 60, 50, 90, 80 ns ; latch 10 ns ; 500 tasks
Find cycle time, one-task time, speedup, and the times for 500 tasks
Formula cycle = slowest + latch ; pipe(n) = (k + n − 1)×cycle ; seq(n) = n × Σphases ; speedup = Σphases / cycle
Cycle    = max(60,50,90,80) + 10 = 90 + 10 = 100 ns
One task = 60 + 50 + 90 + 80 = 280 ns
Speedup  = 280 / 100 = 2.8
Pipe 500 = (4 + 500 - 1) x 100 = 503 x 100 = 50,300 ns
Seq 500  = 500 x 280 = 140,000 ns
Cycle 100 ns; one task 280 ns; speedup 2.8; 500 tasks pipelined 50,300 ns vs sequential 140,000 ns.

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Break it downbefore you compute
Given four stage durations, 60, 50, 90 and 80 ns, a latch delay of 10 ns, and 500 tasks.
Asked six numbers, in the paper's order. Nothing here asks for explanation, so every mark is a figure with its unit.
Marks 6, one per item. Answer all six even if one is guessed: an omitted line cannot score, a wrong line costs only itself.
Taught in Module Two Unit 3, Pipelining.
Trap leaving the latch out of the cycle time. The cycle is the slowest stage plus the latch, 90 + 10 = 100 ns, and every later item depends on it, so one omission poisons five answers. The second trap is the k + n - 1 formula: 500 tasks through 4 stages take 503 cycles, not 504.
Given k = 4 stages · 60, 50, 90, 80 ns · latch = 10 ns · n = 500 tasks
Find cycle time, one-task non-pipelined time, speedup, 500-task pipelined and sequential times, throughput
Formula cycle = slowest + latch · pipelined = (k + n − 1) × cycle · sequential = n × Σstages · throughput = n / pipelined time
Cycle = 90 + 10 = 100 ns. Non-pipelined one task = 60+50+90+80 = 280 ns. Ideal speedup = 280/100 = 2.8. For 500 tasks: pipelined = (4 + 499) × 100 = 50 300 ns; sequential = 500 × 280 = 140 000 ns. Throughput = 500 / 50 300 ns, which in the steady state is one task per cycle, that is 1/100 ns = 10 million tasks per second.

scenario.text: b. i) What is pipelining? 2mks ii) Calculate how long it will take to execute on a regular non-pipelined and pipelined architecture. There are 4 operations with 5 stages each: IF, ID, EX, M and WB; stage1= 8ns, stage2 = 9ns, stage3 = 11ns, stage4 = 13ns, stage5 =16ns. Provide the Gantt Charts for both pipeline and non-pipeline operations. Also calculate the Speedup of the Pipeline system 6mks

questions.asked: Set once, in 2020/2021. It is still the examiner's own question, and the method behind it is on the syllabus.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given four operations, five stages, five stage times, and no latch delay mentioned at all, so take the latch as zero and say that you have.

Asked three deliverables packed into one sentence: the two execution times, the two charts, and the speedup. A student who computes the numbers and draws nothing has left marks that were never about arithmetic.

Marks 2mks for the definition in (i) and 6mks for (ii), which is the largest single part of that question.

Taught in this unit, Module Two Unit 3. Part (i), the definition of pipelining, is the opening paragraph of this unit.

Trap the non-pipelined time is n times the sum of the stages, 4 times 57. The pipelined time uses only the slowest stage, 16 ns, as its clock. Mixing the two is the usual loss here.

exam.problem: Answer 2020/2021 Q1(b) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Given k = 5 stages · stage times = 8, 9, 11, 13, 16 ns · n = 4 operations · no latch delay stated, so take it as 0
Find the non-pipelined time, the pipelined time, and the speedup
Formula cycle = slowest stage · non-pipelined = n × Σ(stage times) · pipelined = (k + n − 1) × cycle · speedup = non-pipelined / pipelined
what each symbol means k = 5 stages · n = 4 operations · Σ(stage times) = 8+9+11+13+16 = 57 ns, the full journey one operation makes without a pipeline · cycle = 16 ns, the slowest stage, because every stage must be given that long
  1. Non-pipelined: each operation passes through all stages, 8+9+11+13+16 = 57 ns each, so 4 × 57 = 228 ns.
  2. Pipelined cycle time = slowest stage = 16 ns.
  3. Pipelined time = (k + n − 1) × cycle = (5 + 4 − 1) × 16 = 8 × 16 = 128 ns.
  4. Speedup = 228 / 128 = 1.78.
Non-pipelined 228 ns, pipelined 128 ns, speedup ≈ 1.78. The speedup is below 5 because only 4 tasks run, so the fill time still dominates.

breakdown.answer:
Given for (i) nothing, it is recall. For (ii) three pairs of floating-point instructions, each pair to be classified.

Asked (i) "Describe the three types". The three names on their own are not a description: each needs the order of the two clashing accesses spelled out. (ii) classify each pair, which is a different skill from reciting the list.

Marks 1½mks for three types, half a mark each, so one short sentence apiece; then 1½ mks for three classifications, again half a mark each.

Taught in this unit, the Teach box directly above.

Trap classifying by instruction name instead of by register. The mnemonic tells you nothing; only the registers do. Write down what each instruction writes and what it reads, then look for the same name on both sides. That method is also the only thing that shows you pair 3 has no overlap at all.

exam.problem: Answer 2020/2021 Q1(c) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
(i)

Read after write (RAW), write after read (WAR), and write after write (WAW). RAW is a true dependency; WAR and WAW are name dependencies that arise when instructions are reordered.

(ii) Take each pair and list what it writes and what it reads. The register, not the mnemonic, decides the answer.

PairWritesReadsRegister in commonHazard
1. MULTD F0, F2, F4
   DIVD F10, F0, F6		 F0
F10		F2, F4
F0, F6		 F0: written first, read secondRAW
2. DIVD F10, F0, F6
   ADDD F6, F8, F2		 F10
F6		F0, F6
F8, F2		 F6: read first, written secondWAR
3. MULTD F0, F2, F4
   SD F8, 50 (R5)		 F0
memory at R5+50		F2, F4
F8, R5		 nonenone as printed
1 is RAW, a true dependency: DIVD needs the F0 that MULTD has not finished writing. 2 is WAR, an anti-dependency: ADDD would overwrite the F6 that DIVD still has to read. 3, as the paper prints it, is no hazard at all: the two instructions touch no register in common.
What to write in the hall. Answer pair 3 the way the page is printed, then add one line: "as printed these two share no register, so there is no data hazard; had the store referenced F0 it would be WAW, write after write." That earns the mark for the analysis and shows the examiner you read the registers rather than pattern matching on the position in the list.
